steps.body: You already know √16 = 4, since 4² = 16. But SOLVING the equation x² = 16 asks something slightly bigger: which numbers, squared, give 16? Both 4² = 16 AND (−4)² = 16 — so x² = 16 has TWO solutions: x = 4 or x = −4, written x = ±4.
Move both x-intercepts until the graph represents x² = 25.

widget.prompt: Build the graph of y = x² − 25 by placing its two crossings. Each crossing is a solution of x² = 25.
widget.successFeedback: The graph crosses at −5 and 5. Both values square to 25, so x² = 25 has two solutions.
widget.shapeFeedback: Set the leading coefficient to 1 so the graph represents x² − 25 rather than a stretched version.
widget.vertexFeedback: Move the two crossings to equal distances on opposite sides of zero: −5 and 5.

predict.prompt: Before moving the crossings, can a negative number squared equal 25?

options.label: Yes; a negative times itself is positive
No; squaring keeps a number negative
Only zero can square to a positive number

predict.reveal: A negative times a negative is positive. Therefore (−5)² and 5² both equal 25, which the two graph crossings make visible.

steps.body: Squaring a positive OR a negative number always gives a positive result (a negative times itself flips back to positive). That's WHY every positive p in x² = p has two solutions, one positive and one negative, that are opposites of each other.

explanationVariants: 7² = 49 and (−7)² = 49, so x² = 49 has solutions x = 7 or x = −7.
Since squaring erases the sign, both 7 and −7 are valid solutions.

commonBuilds.feedback: −7 also works: (−7)² = 49 — don't drop the negative solution.
That's half of 49, not a square root — check 24.5² (much bigger than 49).
49² is way more than 49 — this isn't a solution at all.

widget.missFeedback: Square roots come in ± pairs: both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.

commonErrors.feedback: That's half of 64, not its square root — 8² = 64, so √64 = 8.
4² = 16, not 64 — the square root of 64 is 8, since 8² = 64.

explanationVariants: Isolating gives x² = 36 first, then both signs of its root: x = 6 or x = −6.
Move the −36 over to get x² = 36, then 6² = 36 and (−6)² = 36 both work.

commonBuilds.feedback: −6 also works: isolate first (x² = 36), then both signs of its root square to 36 — don't drop the negative solution.
36 is the constant AFTER isolating (x² = 36), not a solution for x itself. Take the square root of 36: x = ±6.
18 is half of 36 — square roots aren't found by halving. Isolate to x² = 36, then √36 = 6, so x = ±6.

widget.successFeedback: Isolating gives x² = 36 first, then both signs of its root: x = 6 or x = −6.

steps.body: Translate words into the equation first.
explanationVariants: 12 × 12 = 144 and (−12) × (−12) = 144 — translating the words into x² = 144 gives both signs.
"Multiplied by itself" means squared, so this is x² = 144: the number is 12 or −12.

widget.prompt: A number, multiplied by itself, equals 144. What could the number be?

commonBuilds.feedback: −12 also works: (−12) × (−12) = 144 too — don't drop the negative solution.
72 is half of 144, not a square root — check 72 × 72 (far bigger than 144). The number that squares to 144 is 12 (or −12).
144 is the PRODUCT here, not the number itself. Look for what times itself gives 144: 12 (or −12).

widget.missFeedback: "Multiplied by itself" means squared: translate to x² = 144, then both ±12 solve it.
widget.successFeedback: 12 × 12 = 144 and (−12) × (−12) = 144 — translating the words into x² = 144 gives both signs.

widget.prompt: Which equation has the solutions x = 9 and x = −9?

options.label: x² = 81
options.feedback: Right — 9² = 81 and (−9)² = 81, so both ±9 solve x² = 81.

options.label: x² = 18
options.feedback: 18 is 9 + 9, the SUM of the two solutions, not their square. Each solution squares to 81: x² = 81.

options.label: x = 81
options.feedback: x = 81 is a linear equation with only one solution, not the ± pair here. Squaring 9 gives 81: x² = 81.

options.label: x² = 9
options.feedback: 9 is one of the SOLUTIONS, not p itself. Since 9² = 81, the equation is x² = 81, not x² = 9.

steps.body: Not every solution fits the real world.
explanationVariants: 13² = 169, and a rug's side length can't be negative, so only the positive root — 13 feet — is the answer.
Both 13 and −13 solve x² = 169 in pure math, but only the positive length, 13 feet, fits a real rug.

widget.prompt: A square rug has an area of 169 square feet. What is the side length of the rug, in feet?

commonErrors.feedback: −13 solves the pure equation x² = 169, but a rug's side length can't be negative — only the positive root, 13 feet, makes sense here.
84.5 is half of 169, not a square root. The side length is 13 feet, since 13² = 169.
338 doubles 169 rather than finding its square root. Since 13² = 169, the rug's side is 13 feet.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 13² = 169, and since a side length can't be negative, only the positive root — 13 feet — solves this.

hints: 13² = 169, so x = 13 or x = −13 solve the pure equation.
A rug's side length must be positive — only 13 feet makes physical sense.

steps.body: x² = p (for positive p) always has TWO solutions: the positive and negative square root.
takeaways: Squaring erases sign, so both +√p and −√p solve x² = p.
√p alone gives just the positive root; solving x²=p wants both signs.
This only works when p is a perfect square here — otherwise the roots are irrational (recall Chapter 2 of the last course!).
steps.teaser: Next: cube roots — where the story is surprisingly different.

concept.body: Solving x² = p (p a positive perfect square) has TWO solutions: the positive square root AND its negative, since both square to the same positive p.
